# t-Distribution Critical Values

The t distribution is used for inference about a population mean when the population standard deviation, $\sigma$, is unknown and is estimated with the sample standard deviation, $s$. The appropriate critical value depends on:

1. the degrees of freedom;
2. the significance level, $\alpha$; and
3. whether the test is one-tailed or two-tailed.

For a one-sample t test, $df=n-1$. Other t tests use different degrees-of-freedom formulas.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-t-critical
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| tbl-cap: "Positive critical values of the t distribution."

library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

df_values <- c(1:30, 40, 60, 80, 100, 120, Inf)
alpha_values <- c(0.05, 0.01, 0.001)

one_tailed <- sapply(
  alpha_values,
  function(alpha) ifelse(
    is.infinite(df_values),
    qnorm(1 - alpha),
    qt(1 - alpha, df_values)
  )
)

two_tailed <- sapply(
  alpha_values,
  function(alpha) ifelse(
    is.infinite(df_values),
    qnorm(1 - alpha / 2),
    qt(1 - alpha / 2, df_values)
  )
)

t_table <- data.frame(
  df = ifelse(is.infinite(df_values), "∞ (z)", as.character(df_values)),
  round(cbind(one_tailed, two_tailed), 3),
  check.names = FALSE
)

names(t_table) <- c(
  "df",
  rep(c("α = .05", "α = .01", "α = .001"), 2)
)

t_output <- kable(
  t_table,
  booktabs = TRUE,
  align = "ccccccc"
)

t_output <- add_header_above(
  t_output,
  c(" " = 1, "One-Tailed Test" = 3, "Two-Tailed Test" = 3)
)

if (knitr::is_latex_output()) {
  t_output <- kable_styling(
    t_output,
    latex_options = c("hold_position", "repeat_header"),
    font_size = 8
  )
} else {
  t_output <- kable_styling(t_output, full_width = FALSE)
}

t_output
```

## Using the Table

- For a **right-tailed test**, use the positive critical value shown in the one-tailed section.
- For a **left-tailed test**, use the negative of the listed one-tailed value.
- For a **two-tailed test**, compare the absolute obtained statistic, $|t|$, with the positive value in the two-tailed section.
- For a confidence interval with confidence level $1-\alpha$, use the corresponding two-tailed critical value.
- If the exact degrees of freedom are not listed, use the next smaller listed value as a conservative classroom approximation.
- Welch's t test can produce noninteger degrees of freedom. Round down when using this printed table unless instructed to use software.

::: {.callout-important title="Select the column before examining the result"}
The research hypothesis determines whether a test is one-tailed or two-tailed. Do not select the tail after seeing the sample result.
:::

## Worked Example

Suppose a one-sample test has $n=6$, so:

$$
df=n-1=5
$$

For a right-tailed test with $\alpha=.05$, locate row $df=5$ and the one-tailed $\alpha=.05$ column. The critical value is approximately:

$$
t_{critical}=2.015
$$

Reject the null hypothesis only if the obtained t statistic is greater than 2.015. For a left-tailed test, the corresponding critical value would be $-2.015$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-t-critical-example
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: "Right-tail rejection region for df = 5 and alpha = .05."
#| fig-alt: "t distribution with five degrees of freedom and the right tail beyond 2.015 shaded."
#| fig-height: 2.6
#| fig-width: 6

library(ggplot2)

example_df <- 5
example_alpha <- 0.05
t_critical <- qt(1 - example_alpha, example_df)
t_data <- data.frame(t = seq(-5, 5, length.out = 1600))
t_data$density <- dt(t_data$t, df = example_df)
t_tail <- subset(t_data, t >= t_critical)

ggplot(t_data, aes(x = t, y = density)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_area(
    data = t_tail,
    fill = "grey65",
    color = "black",
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = t_critical, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = 2.9, y = 0.035, label = "α = .05") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-4, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2.015, 3, 4)) +
  labs(x = "t", y = "Density") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 11)
```

The final row, $df=\infty$, gives the corresponding standard normal critical values. As degrees of freedom increase, the t distribution approaches the standard normal distribution.
